claim: Tauopathies are neurodegenerative diseases characterized by aberrant forms of tau protein accumulation leading to neuronal death in focal brain areas.
source: Tauopathies are neurodegenerative diseases characterized by aberrant forms of tau protein accumulation leading to neuronal death in focal brain areas.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about tauopathies that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Positron emission tomography (PET) tracers that bind to pathological tau are used in diagnosis.
source: Positron emission tomography (PET) tracers that bind to pathological tau are used in diagnosis, but there are no current therapies to eliminate these tau species.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical practice in the field of tauopathy diagnosis.

claim: There are no current therapies to eliminate pathological tau species.
source: Positron emission tomography (PET) tracers that bind to pathological tau are used in diagnosis, but there are no current therapies to eliminate these tau species.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of therapeutic development in the field.

claim: QC-01-175 is a hetero-bifunctional molecule designed to engage both tau and Cereblon (CRBN).
source: The hetero-bifunctional molecule QC-01–175 was designed to engage both tau and Cereblon (CRBN), a substrate-receptor for the E3-ubiquitin ligase CRL4CRBN, to trigger tau ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
evidence: The design and structure of QC-01-175 is described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: QC-01-175 was designed to trigger tau ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: The hetero-bifunctional molecule QC-01–175 was designed to engage both tau and Cereblon (CRBN), a substrate-receptor for the E3-ubiquitin ligase CRL4CRBN, to trigger tau ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
evidence: The intended mechanism of action is described based on the design principles of PROTACs.

claim: QC-01-175 effected clearance of tau in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patient-derived neuronal cell models.
source: QC-01–175 effected clearance of tau in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patient-derived neuronal cell models, with minimal effect on tau from neurons of healthy controls, indicating specificity for disease-relevant forms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, including western blots, ELISAs, and immunofluorescence.

claim: QC-01-175 had minimal effect on tau from neurons of healthy controls.
source: QC-01–175 effected clearance of tau in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patient-derived neuronal cell models, with minimal effect on tau from neurons of healthy controls, indicating specificity for disease-relevant forms.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2H-J comparing FTD neurons to control neurons.

claim: QC-01-175 shows specificity for disease-relevant forms of tau.
source: QC-01–175 effected clearance of tau in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patient-derived neuronal cell models, with minimal effect on tau from neurons of healthy controls, indicating specificity for disease-relevant forms.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effect on FTD neurons versus control neurons shown in Figure 2.

claim: QC-01-175 rescued stress vulnerability in FTD neurons.
source: QC-01–175 also rescued stress vulnerability in FTD neurons, phenocopying CRISPR-mediated MAPT-knockout.
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: QC-01-175 phenocopies CRISPR-mediated MAPT-knockout in rescuing stress vulnerability.
source: QC-01–175 also rescued stress vulnerability in FTD neurons, phenocopying CRISPR-mediated MAPT-knockout.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of QC-01-175 effect to MAPT KO in Figure 7C.

claim: Aberrant tau in FTD patient-derived neurons is amenable to targeted degradation.
source: This work demonstrates that aberrant tau in FTD patient-derived neurons is amenable to targeted degradation, representing an important advance for therapeutics.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results showing tau degradation in FTD neurons.

claim: Tauopathies include frontotemporal dementia (FTD), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Tauopathies, such as frontotemporal dementia (FTD), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), are a group of neurodegenerative diseases characterized by the pathological accumulation of hyper-phosphorylated tau (P-tau) protein, in the form of intracellular paired helical filaments (PHFs) or neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), within neurons and glia of affected brain regions, leading to cell death (Kosik et al., 1989; Morris et al., 2011; Cruts and Van Broeckhoven, 2015; Ghetti et al., 2015; Neumann et al., 2015; Olney et al., 2017; Goedert, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Tauopathies are characterized by pathological accumulation of hyper-phosphorylated tau (P-tau) protein in the form of intracellular paired helical filaments (PHFs) or neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs).
source: Tauopathies, such as frontotemporal dementia (FTD), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), are a group of neurodegenerative diseases characterized by the pathological accumulation of hyper-phosphorylated tau (P-tau) protein, in the form of intracellular paired helical filaments (PHFs) or neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), within neurons and glia of affected brain regions, leading to cell death (Kosik et al., 1989; Morris et al., 2011; Cruts and Van Broeckhoven, 2015; Ghetti et al., 2015; Neumann et al., 2015; Olney et al., 2017; Goedert, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Pathological tau accumulation occurs within neurons and glia of affected brain regions.
source: Tauopathies, such as frontotemporal dementia (FTD), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), are a group of neurodegenerative diseases characterized by the pathological accumulation of hyper-phosphorylated tau (P-tau) protein, in the form of intracellular paired helical filaments (PHFs) or neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), within neurons and glia of affected brain regions, leading to cell death (Kosik et al., 1989; Morris et al., 2011; Cruts and Van Broeckhoven, 2015; Ghetti et al., 2015; Neumann et al., 2015; Olney et al., 2017; Goedert, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Tauopathies can be either sporadic or inherited as autosomal dominant disease when caused by mutations in the MAPT gene.
source: Tauopathies can be either sporadic or inherited as autosomal dominant disease when caused by mutations in the MAPT gene encoding the microtubule-associated protein tau.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the genetic basis of tauopathies.

claim: FTD is the most common form of dementia in individuals under 60 years of age.
source: FTD is the most common form of dementia in individuals under 60 years of age, affecting approximately 60,000 individuals in the USA alone, with an economic burden that is nearly twice that reported for AD (Galvin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galvin et al., 2017.

claim: FTD affects approximately 60,000 individuals in the USA.
source: FTD is the most common form of dementia in individuals under 60 years of age, affecting approximately 60,000 individuals in the USA alone, with an economic burden that is nearly twice that reported for AD (Galvin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galvin et al., 2017.

claim: The economic burden of FTD is nearly twice that reported for AD.
source: FTD is the most common form of dementia in individuals under 60 years of age, affecting approximately 60,000 individuals in the USA alone, with an economic burden that is nearly twice that reported for AD (Galvin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galvin et al., 2017.

claim: There are currently no effective disease-modifying therapies for FTD.
source: Despite its devastating effects, there are currently no effective disease-modifying therapies, highlighting an urgent unmet need.
evidence: This reflects the current state of therapeutic development for FTD.

claim: Molecular mechanisms leading to neuronal toxicity and death in tauopathies are still not entirely understood.
source: One of the major bottlenecks in developing effective therapies for tauopathies resides in the fact that molecular mechanisms leading to neuronal toxicity and death are still not entirely understood (Congdon and Sigurdsson, 2018; Panza et al., 2016; Medina, 2018; Götz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to review articles.

claim: Early tau post-translational modifications lead to misfolding, mislocalization, oligomerization, and changes in solubility.
source: Cumulative evidence from murine tauopathy models and postmortem patient brain studies suggests that early tau post-translational modifications lead to misfolding, mislocalization, oligomerization, and changes in solubility.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies in mouse models and human postmortem tissue.

claim: Early tau modifications appear to be determinant toxicity effectors.
source: These events appear to be determinant toxicity effectors (Johnson and Stoothoff, 2004; Min et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Götz et al., 2013; Kopeikina et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2013; Yanamandra et al., 2013; Cowan and Mudher, 2013), whereas tau tangles alone are not sufficient to cause neuronal death (Cowan and Mudher, 2013; de Calignon et al., 2010; Kopeikina et al., 2012; Santacruz et al., 2005; Spires et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies examining tau toxicity.

claim: Tau tangles alone are not sufficient to cause neuronal death.
source: These events appear to be determinant toxicity effectors (Johnson and Stoothoff, 2004; Min et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Götz et al., 2013; Kopeikina et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2013; Yanamandra et al., 2013; Cowan and Mudher, 2013), whereas tau tangles alone are not sufficient to cause neuronal death (Cowan and Mudher, 2013; de Calignon et al., 2010; Kopeikina et al., 2012; Santacruz et al., 2005; Spires et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies examining the relationship between tangles and neuronal death.

claim: Targeting early forms of toxic tau for clearance may be a promising therapeutic strategy to reduce neuronal degeneration.
source: Therefore, targeting early forms of toxic tau for clearance may facilitate the study of their role in disease etiology and be a promising therapeutic strategy to reduce neuronal degeneration.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the evidence that early tau modifications are toxic while tangles are not sufficient for death.

claim: A challenge in developing cell-permeable small molecules that target tau is the lack of a well-defined tau fold and active sites in disease.
source: A challenge in developing cell-permeable small molecules that target tau is the lack of a well-defined tau fold and active sites, in disease.
evidence: This reflects a known challenge in the field of tau drug discovery.

claim: Current investigative tau-directed therapeutics have focused on aggregation inhibitors.
source: Current investigative tau-directed therapeutics have focused on aggregation inhibitors (Brunden et al., 2010; Panza et al., 2016; Bulic et al., 2009), activators of protein clearance through autophagy (Boland et al., 2008; Krüger et al., 2012; Medina, 2018; Wang and Mandelkow, 2012; Rubinsztein et al., 2015), and inhibition of tau kinases (Dolan and Johnson, 2010; Medina, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on different therapeutic approaches.

claim: Current investigative tau-directed therapeutics have focused on activators of protein clearance through autophagy.
source: Current investigative tau-directed therapeutics have focused on aggregation inhibitors (Brunden et al., 2010; Panza et al., 2016; Bulic et al., 2009), activators of protein clearance through autophagy (Boland et al., 2008; Krüger et al., 2012; Medina, 2018; Wang and Mandelkow, 2012; Rubinsztein et al., 2015), and inhibition of tau kinases (Dolan and Johnson, 2010; Medina, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on autophagy activation.

claim: Current investigative tau-directed therapeutics have focused on inhibition of tau kinases.
source: Current investigative tau-directed therapeutics have focused on aggregation inhibitors (Brunden et al., 2010; Panza et al., 2016; Bulic et al., 2009), activators of protein clearance through autophagy (Boland et al., 2008; Krüger et al., 2012; Medina, 2018; Wang and Mandelkow, 2012; Rubinsztein et al., 2015), and inhibition of tau kinases (Dolan and Johnson, 2010; Medina, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on tau kinase inhibition.

claim: Anti-tau immunotherapy has shown promise in animal models.
source: Moreover, anti-tau immunotherapy has shown promise in animal models, but antibody affinity and specificity as well as strong immune responses pose critical challenges (Gu et al., 2013; Panza et al., 2016; Pedersen and Sigurdsson, 2015; Novak et al., 2017; Yanamandra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on tau immunotherapy.

claim: Antibody affinity and specificity as well as strong immune responses pose critical challenges for anti-tau immunotherapy.
source: Moreover, anti-tau immunotherapy has shown promise in animal models, but antibody affinity and specificity as well as strong immune responses pose critical challenges (Gu et al., 2013; Panza et al., 2016; Pedersen and Sigurdsson, 2015; Novak et al., 2017; Yanamandra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies discussing challenges with immunotherapy.

claim: Anti-sense oligonucleotides (ASO) to decrease tau expression led to reversal of tau pathology in mouse and non-human primate models.
source: An alternative and promising strategy has focused on using anti-sense oligonucleotides (ASO) to decrease tau expression, leading to reversal of tau pathology in mouse and non-human primate models (DeVos et al., 2017; Mignon et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ASO approaches.

claim: Developing small molecule agents that target early forms of toxic tau and result in their degradation may represent a uniquely advantageous strategy for halting tauopathies.
source: Still, given potential limitations with existing approaches, developing small molecule agents that target early forms of toxic tau, and result in their degradation, may represent a uniquely advantageous strategy for halting tauopathies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential advantages of the degrader approach.

claim: Targeted protein degradation approaches have expanded the landscape of druggable proteins by providing a mechanism to transform a non-functional protein binder into an effective targeted degrader.
source: Targeted protein degradation approaches have expanded the landscape of druggable proteins by providing a mechanism to transform a non-functional protein binder into an effective targeted degrader (Gechijian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gechijian et al., 2018.

claim: Targeted protein degraders (PROTACs) are an emerging strategy for ablating previously undruggable protein functions.
source: Targeted protein degraders, also known as PROTACs (PROteolysis TArgeting Chimeras), are an emerging strategy for ablating previously undruggable protein functions (Cromm et al., 2018; Gechijian et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2014; Lai and Crews, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to PROTAC literature.

claim: Degraders are hetero-bivalent compounds where a small molecule binder of the protein of interest is linked via a short linker to an E3-ligase recruiting molecule.
source: Structurally, degraders are hetero-bivalent compounds where a small molecule binder of the protein of interest is linked via a short linker to an E3-ligase recruiting molecule, such as the CRBN binder thalidomide (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a structural description of degraders, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Degraders result in ternary complex formation between the protein of interest, the degrader molecule and the E3-ligase complex.
source: This results in ternary complex formation between the protein of interest, the degrader molecule and the E3-ligase complex, in this case CUL4-RBX1-DDB1-CRBN (CRL4CRBN), and induces ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of the protein of interest (Figure 1B) (Fischer et al., 2014; Krönke et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Chamberlain et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2017; Metzger et al., 2014).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Ternary complex formation induces ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of the protein of interest.
source: This results in ternary complex formation between the protein of interest, the degrader molecule and the E3-ligase complex, in this case CUL4-RBX1-DDB1-CRBN (CRL4CRBN), and induces ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of the protein of interest (Figure 1B) (Fischer et al., 2014; Krönke et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Chamberlain et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2017; Metzger et al., 2014).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: A tau degrader molecule was designed based on the T807 core scaffold for tau recognition.
source: QC-01–175 (I) was synthesized based on the T807 core scaffold for tau recognition, a thalidomide analog E3 ligand (pomalidomide) for CRBN engagement, and a linker designed for maximum target clearance efficiency (II).
evidence: The design and synthesis of QC-01-175 is described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: QC-01-175 contains pomalidomide for CRBN engagement.
source: QC-01–175 (I) was synthesized based on the T807 core scaffold for tau recognition, a thalidomide analog E3 ligand (pomalidomide) for CRBN engagement, and a linker designed for maximum target clearance efficiency (II).
evidence: The structure of QC-01-175 is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: QC-01-175 contains a linker designed for maximum target clearance efficiency.
source: QC-01–175 (I) was synthesized based on the T807 core scaffold for tau recognition, a thalidomide analog E3 ligand (pomalidomide) for CRBN engagement, and a linker designed for maximum target clearance efficiency (II).
evidence: The design rationale is described in the text and the structure is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: QC-03-075 is the inactive analog of QC-01-175.
source: QC-03–075 is the inactive analog (III).
evidence: The structure of QC-03-075 is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In vitro, QC-01-175 binds to variant forms of tau within the same order of magnitude as T807.
source: BLI results indicate that, in vitro, QC-01–175 binds to variant forms of tau within the same order of magnitude as T807.
evidence: This is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: QC-01-175 binds to wild-type tau with a KD of 1.2 μM in vitro.
source: In this in vitro format, although weaker binding was observed compared to PE859 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), QC-01–175 was able to bind to immobilized, soluble forms of WT (KD1.2 μM), A152T (KD1.7 μM) and P301L (KD2.5 μM) within the same order of magnitude as the control T807 (KD1.8 µM, 2.1 μM and 1.7 μM, respectively) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B III, VI).
evidence: This is supported by BLI measurements shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: QC-01-175 binds to tau-A152T with a KD of 1.7 μM in vitro.
source: In this in vitro format, although weaker binding was observed compared to PE859 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), QC-01–175 was able to bind to immobilized, soluble forms of WT (KD1.2 μM), A152T (KD1.7 μM) and P301L (KD2.5 μM) within the same order of magnitude as the control T807 (KD1.8 µM, 2.1 μM and 1.7 μM, respectively) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B III, VI).
evidence: This is supported by BLI measurements shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: QC-01-175 binds to tau-P301L with a KD of 2.5 μM in vitro.
source: In this in vitro format, although weaker binding was observed compared to PE859 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), QC-01–175 was able to bind to immobilized, soluble forms of WT (KD1.2 μM), A152T (KD1.7 μM) and P301L (KD2.5 μM) within the same order of magnitude as the control T807 (KD1.8 µM, 2.1 μM and 1.7 μM, respectively) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B III, VI).
evidence: This is supported by BLI measurements shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: T807 binds to wild-type tau with a KD of 1.8 μM in vitro.
source: In this in vitro format, although weaker binding was observed compared to PE859 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), QC-01–175 was able to bind to immobilized, soluble forms of WT (KD1.2 μM), A152T (KD1.7 μM) and P301L (KD2.5 μM) within the same order of magnitude as the control T807 (KD1.8 µM, 2.1 μM and 1.7 μM, respectively) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B III, VI).
evidence: This is supported by BLI measurements shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In vitro QC-01-175 and T807 displayed significantly lower affinity for all recombinant immobilized tau forms than the reported KD of T807 for native, aggregated tau filaments from AD brain sections (KD 15 nM).
source: As expected, in vitro QC-01–175 and T807 displayed a significantly lower affinity for all recombinant immobilized tau forms than the reported KD of T807 for native, aggregated tau filaments from AD brain sections (KD15 nM) (Chien et al., 2013; Gobbi et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2013).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to studies measuring T807 binding to AD brain tissue.

claim: The lower affinity of QC-01-175 for recombinant tau compared to aggregated tau suggests that QC-01-175 may exhibit conformational selectivity similar to T807.
source: This property enables T807-based PET tracers to distinguish pathological tau species from the functional tau found in cells, and suggested that QC-01–175 may exhibit similar conformational selectivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data and known properties of T807.

claim: T807 and derivatives have low affinity for monomeric, soluble protein, independent of the presence of a tau variant.
source: Comparison between binding of recombinant WT protein and variant tau forms, to either QC-01–175 or the controls PE859 and T807, indicates that T807 and derivatives have low affinity for monomeric, soluble protein, independent of the presence of a tau variant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The PET tracer 18F-T807 has off-target activity against monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) and monoamine oxidase-A (MAO-A).
source: The PET tracer 18F-T807 has off-target activity against monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) and monoamine oxidase-A (MAO-A) (Lemoine et al., 2018; Vermeiren et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on T807 off-target effects.

claim: QC-01-175 showed reduced inhibition of MAO relative to T807 (IC50 8.56 μM vs 0.14 μM, respectively).
source: QC-01–175 showed reduced inhibition of MAO relative to T807 (IC508.56 μM vs 0.14 μM, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MAO activity assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Post-mitotic neurons were generated from patients' induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived cortical-enriched neural progenitor cells (NPCs) subsequently differentiated into neurons for a period of 6 to 8 weeks.
source: Post-mitotic neurons were generated from patients' induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived cortical-enriched neural progenitor cells (NPCs) subsequently differentiated into neurons for a period of 6 to 8 weeks, as previously described (Cheng et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2016; Seo et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the cell culture methods used, supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Patient-specific cellular models express tau at endogenous levels and recapitulate disease-relevant tau phenotypes ex vivo.
source: These patient-specific cellular models that express tau at endogenous levels, recapitulate disease-relevant tau phenotypes ex vivo (Fong et al., 2013; Silva et al., 2016) and present a valuable opportunity to test emerging therapeutics directly against a clinically relevant model of human disease (Dolmetsch and Geschwind, 2011; Silva et al., 2017; Wan et al., 2015; Inoue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing these cellular models.

claim: In A152T neurons treated with QC-01-175 for 24 hr, a concentration-dependent reduction in total tau and P-tau levels was observed by western blotting analysis.
source: In A152T neurons treated with QC-01–175 for 24 hr (Figure 2A), we observed a concentration-dependent reduction in total tau and P-tau levels by western blotting analysis (Figure 2B) and by tau ELISAs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In A152T neurons treated with QC-01-175 for 24 hr, a concentration-dependent reduction in total tau and P-tau levels was observed by tau ELISAs.
source: In A152T neurons treated with QC-01–175 for 24 hr (Figure 2A), we observed a concentration-dependent reduction in total tau and P-tau levels by western blotting analysis (Figure 2B) and by tau ELISAs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: P-tauS396 and high-molecular-weight P-tauS396 were effectively degraded at concentrations as low as 100 nM QC-01-175.
source: P-tauS396 and high-molecular-weight P-tauS396, identified as SDS-insoluble bands > 250 kDa (Figure 2B), were effectively degraded at concentrations as low as 100 nM QC-01–175, whereas maximal total tau clearance (Dmax, 24h) was achieved at 10 μM, consistent with expected binding preference of a T807-derivative for insoluble P-tau (Chien et al., 2013; Lowe et al., 2016; Marquié et al., 2015; Xia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Maximal total tau clearance (Dmax, 24h) was achieved at 10 μM QC-01-175.
source: P-tauS396 and high-molecular-weight P-tauS396, identified as SDS-insoluble bands > 250 kDa (Figure 2B), were effectively degraded at concentrations as low as 100 nM QC-01–175, whereas maximal total tau clearance (Dmax, 24h) was achieved at 10 μM, consistent with expected binding preference of a T807-derivative for insoluble P-tau (Chien et al., 2013; Lowe et al., 2016; Marquié et al., 2015; Xia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The observed Dmax, 24h of 75% for total tau and of 85% for P-tau S396 was well above the 50% mutant tau allele expressed by heterozygous neurons.
source: The observed Dmax, 24h of 75% for total tau and of 85% for P-tau S396, averaged across independent replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), was well above the 50% mutant tau allele expressed by heterozygous neurons, indicating that both variant and WT forms of tau are recognized and degraded.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both variant and WT forms of tau are recognized and degraded by QC-01-175.
source: The observed Dmax, 24h of 75% for total tau and of 85% for P-tau S396, averaged across independent replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), was well above the 50% mutant tau allele expressed by heterozygous neurons, indicating that both variant and WT forms of tau are recognized and degraded.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that degradation exceeds 50% in heterozygous neurons.

claim: Tau-A152T and tau-WT accumulate in similar proportions in A152T neurons.
source: Previous mass spectrometry (MS) FLEXITau analysis demonstrated that tau-A152T and tau-WT accumulate in similar proportions in these neurons (Silva et al., 2016), suggesting that QC-01–175 targets pathogenic tau conformations that include both WT and A152T tau, rather than tau variant exclusively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silva et al., 2016.

claim: QC-01-175 targets pathogenic tau conformations that include both WT and A152T tau, rather than tau variant exclusively.
source: Previous mass spectrometry (MS) FLEXITau analysis demonstrated that tau-A152T and tau-WT accumulate in similar proportions in these neurons (Silva et al., 2016), suggesting that QC-01–175 targets pathogenic tau conformations that include both WT and A152T tau, rather than tau variant exclusively.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that degradation exceeds 50% and both tau forms are present in equal amounts.

claim: QC-01-175 promoted between 50 and 100% tau clearance across nine independent experiments, a statistically significant reduction relative to vehicle.
source: To ascertain this inherent variability, we plotted the levels of total tau and P-tauS396 upon 24 hr treatment with 1 μM or 10 μM doses of QC-01–175 across nine independent experiments. QC-01–175 promoted between 50 and 100% tau clearance, a statistically significant reduction relative to vehicle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The negative control QC-03-075 showed no effect on the levels of total tau and P-tauS396 at all concentrations tested.
source: Conversely, the negative control QC-03–075 (Figure 2D) showed no effect on the levels of total tau and P-tauS396 at all concentrations tested, indicating that engagement with CRL4CRBN is required for QC-01–175-mediated tau clearance (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 2E, 2F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Engagement with CRL4CRBN is required for QC-01-175-mediated tau clearance.
source: Conversely, the negative control QC-03–075 (Figure 2D) showed no effect on the levels of total tau and P-tauS396 at all concentrations tested, indicating that engagement with CRL4CRBN is required for QC-01–175-mediated tau clearance (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of the negative control QC-03-075, which cannot bind CRBN.

claim: Immunofluorescence of A152T neurons showed a clear reduction in tau and P-tau S396/S404 after treatment with 10 μM QC-01-175 for 24 hr relative to vehicle- or QC-03-075-treated neurons.
source: We employed immunofluorescence (IF) of tau in A152T neurons to assess the effect of treatment with 10 μM QC-01–175 for 24 hr. Total tau (K9JA antibody), P-tauS396/S404 (PHF-1 antibody) and neuronal marker MAP2 were imaged, and a clear reduction in tau and P-tau S396/S404 were observed relative to vehicle- or QC-03–075-treated neurons (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 2G.

claim: QC-01-175 effected concentration-dependent degradation of total and P-tauS396 in tau-P301L neurons at the 24 hr time point, with a Dmax, 24h of 60% achieved at 1 μM compound.
source: Next, we tested whether QC-01–175 could degrade multiple FTD-relevant tau species by repeating the ELISA tau quantification assay in tau-P301L neurons. QC-01–175 effected concentration-dependent degradation of total and P-tauS396 at the 24 hr time point, with a Dmax, 24h of 60% achieved at 1 μM compound for both tau species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 24 hr treatment with 1 μM QC-01-175 resulted in a 70% reduction in total tau and an 80% reduction of P-tauS396 in P301L neurons.
source: These effects were corroborated by western blotting analysis, where 24 hr treatment with 1 μM QC-01–175 resulted in a 70% reduction in total tau and an 80% reduction of P-tauS396, comparable to the effect in A152T neurons, whereas QC-03–075 had no effect on the levels of either tau species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: No significant degradation of tau or P-tauS396 was observed after 24 hr treatment with either QC-01-175 or negative control QC-03-075 at concentrations up to 1 μM in all three control neurons.
source: To investigate the ability of QC-01–175 to discriminate between normal and disease-associated tau, we tested our degrader against three independent, non-affected iPSC-derived neuronal cell models expressing WT tau, control neurons 1–3, in a tau ELISA assay (Figure 2—source data 1). These control neuronal cultures also contain reduced levels of the low-solubility P-tauS396 species present in the FTD-patient-derived neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C vs. A, B) (Silva et al., 2016). No significant degradation of tau or P-tauS396 was observed after 24 hr treatment with either QC-01–175 or negative control QC-03–075 at concentrations up to 1 μM in all three control neurons (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2H-J.

claim: 1 μM QC-01-175 was unable to induce significant degradation of tau or P-tau after 24 hr in control line 1.
source: We corroborated these results by western blotting, where 1 μM QC-01–175 was unable to induce significant degradation of tau or P-tau after 24 hr in control line 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At the highest dose of 10 μM, QC-01-175 induced ~20% degradation of total tau in two of the control lines (1 and 2) and had no effect in the third line.
source: At the highest dose of 10 μM, QC-01–175 induced ~20% degradation of total tau in two of the control lines (1 and 2) and had no effect in the third line.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2H-J.

claim: 10 μM QC-01-175 degraded ~40% of P-tauS396 in control line 1 and had no significant effect in control lines 2 and 3.
source: Similarly, 10 μM QC-01–175 degraded ~40% of P-tauS396 in control line 1 and had no significant effect in control lines 2 and 3.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2H-J.

claim: QC-01-175 is significantly more effective at inducing degradation of the forms of tau present in FTD patient-derived neurons compared to control neurons.
source: Comparative analysis of the effect of QC-01–175 across all cell lines tested suggests that QC-01–175 is significantly more effective at inducing degradation of the forms of tau present in FTD patient-derived neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Excess lenalidomide or T807 reversed QC-01-175-mediated tau degradation in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: First, excess lenalidomide or T807 that saturate ligand binding sites of CRBN or tau, respectively (Figure 3A), reversed QC-01–175-mediated tau degradation in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: Pre-treatment with MLN4924 caused a concentration-dependent rescue of the effect of QC-01-175.
source: Next, pre-treatment with MLN4924 (Pevonedistat), which inhibits NAE (neddylation activating enzyme NEDD8, and therefore neddylation 'N' of CUL4) (Lan et al., 2016) and consequently E3 ligase activity (Figure 3B), or pre-treatment with the irreversible proteasome inhibitor carfilzomib (Figure 3C) (Huang and Dixit, 2016), caused a concentration-dependent rescue of the effect of QC-01–175 (Figure 3B,C,E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B and 3E.

claim: Pre-treatment with carfilzomib caused a concentration-dependent rescue of the effect of QC-01-175.
source: Next, pre-treatment with MLN4924 (Pevonedistat), which inhibits NAE (neddylation activating enzyme NEDD8, and therefore neddylation 'N' of CUL4) (Lan et al., 2016) and consequently E3 ligase activity (Figure 3B), or pre-treatment with the irreversible proteasome inhibitor carfilzomib (Figure 3C) (Huang and Dixit, 2016), caused a concentration-dependent rescue of the effect of QC-01–175 (Figure 3B,C,E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and 3F.

claim: The autophagy inhibitor bafilomycin A1 did not reverse the degrader effect and further promoted tau clearance.
source: In contrast, the autophagy inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (Baf.A1) did not reverse the degrader effect and further promoted tau clearance, possibly as a compensatory response between autophagy and proteasome clearance pathways (Figure 3B,E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B and 3E.

claim: QC-01-175 did not significantly affect the levels of CRBN by 24 hr.
source: We also confirmed that QC-01–175 did not significantly affect the levels of CRBN by 24 hr, which remained constant across all concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: QC-01-175-mediated tau degradation is dependent on CRBN and tau binding, neddylation (E3 ligase function) and proteasome function, but not autophagy.
source: Taken together, these data establish that QC-01–175-mediated tau degradation is dependent on CRBN and tau binding, neddylation (E3 ligase function) and proteasome function, but not autophagy, consistent with the proposed mechanism of action (Figure 1B).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of DDB1 showed co-IP with both total tau (TAU5) and P-tau (PHF-1) upon QC-01-175 treatment ±carfilzomib.
source: Immunoprecipitation of DDB1 and follow-up western blotting analysis showed co-IP with both total tau (TAU5) and P-tau (PHF-1) upon QC-01–175 treatment ±carfilzomib (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is some basal interaction between tau and the CRL4CRBN E3 ligase in vehicle and negative control QC-03-075 treated samples.
source: There was also a weak detection of total tau and P-tau in vehicle and negative control QC-03–075 treated samples, suggesting that some basal interaction between tau and the CRL4CRBN E3 ligase may also occur endogenously in human neurons, as has been reported in tissue from mouse brain (David et al., 2002; Del Prete et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from co-IP data shown in Figure 4A and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Probing with an ubiquitin antibody showed an increase in ubiquitinated proteins by QC-01-175 ± carfilzomib treatment, with the same migration as tau (~50 kDa).
source: Probing with an ubiquitin antibody (W:Ubi-1, Figure 4A) showed an increase in ubiquitinated proteins by QC-01–175 ± carfilzomib treatment, with the same migration as tau (~50 kDa), consistent with a QC-01–175-mediated increase in tau ubiquitination.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of tau showed co-IP with CRBN in QC-01-175 treated samples ± carfilzomib or bortezomib.
source: Conversely, immunoprecipitation of tau (TAU5 antibody) and western blotting analysis showed co-IP with CRBN in QC-01–175 treated samples ± carfilzomib or bortezomib (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CUL4A and DDB1 were detected by western blotting in tau immunoprecipitation samples, particularly in carfilzomib- and bortezomib-treated samples.
source: CUL4A and DDB1 were also detected by western blotting, particularly in carfilzomib- and bortezomib-treated samples, but at much lower intensity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The co-IP results support ternary complex formation between tau, degrader and CRL4CRBN followed by increased tau ubiquitination at the 4 hr time point.
source: These results support ternary complex formation between tau, degrader and CRL4CRBN followed by increased tau ubiquitination, at the 4 hr time point, providing further evidence of the mechanism of tau clearance by QC-01–175 through E3 ligase function and proteasome degradation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the co-IP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the 4 hr time-point in A152T neurons, maximum clearance of tau and P-tauS396 (Dmax, 4h = 80%) was observed at 100 nM QC-01-175.
source: For A152T neurons, at the 4 hr time-point we observed a sharp hook effect (Huang and Dixit, 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), with maximum clearance of tau and P-tauS396 (Dmax, 4h = 80%) at 100 nM (Figure 5A–B), constant 50% degradation at 500 nM and 1 μM (Figure 5C), and little effect on tau levels at 10 μM QC-01–175 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A hook effect was observed at the 4 hr time-point in A152T neurons treated with QC-01-175.
source: For A152T neurons, at the 4 hr time-point we observed a sharp hook effect (Huang and Dixit, 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), with maximum clearance of tau and P-tauS396 (Dmax, 4h = 80%) at 100 nM (Figure 5A–B), constant 50% degradation at 500 nM and 1 μM (Figure 5C), and little effect on tau levels at 10 μM QC-01–175 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After 8 hr treatment with QC-01-175, the hook effect lessened in A152T neurons.
source: After 8 hr, the hook effect lessened (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and Dmax, 8h of 50% tau was observed at all concentrations above 100 nM (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At the 24 hr time-point, tau and P-tauS396 levels were further reduced in a concentration-dependent manner to a Dmax, 24h of 70% at 10 μM in A152T neurons.
source: By comparison, at the 24 hr time-point tau and P-tauS396 levels were further reduced in a concentration-dependent manner to a Dmax, 24h of 70% at 10 μM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In P301L neurons at the 4 hr time-point, Dmax, 4h for total tau occurred at 100 nM, whereas for P-tauS396 maximal degradation was observed at 500 nM (both Dmax, 4h = 80%).
source: In P310L neurons, there was more variability between the two tau species at the 4 hr time-point (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F). For total tau, we observed a hook effect with Dmax, 4h occurring at 100 nM, whereas for P-tauS396 maximal degradation was observed at 500 nM (both Dmax, 4h = 80%).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: By 8 hr, robust degradation of tau and P-tauS396 (40-50%) was achieved at all concentrations above 500 nM in P301L neurons.
source: However, by 8 hr robust degradation of tau and P-tauS396(40–50%) was achieved at all concentrations above 500 nM, and Dmax, 8h was further increased to 60–70% by 24 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Upon 4 hr treatment with 1 μM QC-01-175, the only significant changes observed in the A152T neuronal proteome comprise the validated immune-modulatory drug (IMiD) targets ZFP91, ZNF653 and ZNF827.
source: Upon 4 hr treatment with 1 μM QC-01–175, the only significant changes observed comprise the validated immune-modulatory drug (IMiD) targets ZFP91, ZNF653 and ZNF827 (Donovan et al., 2018), while no QC-01–175 specific off-targets were observed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Degradation of ZFP91, ZNF653 and ZNF827 was expected as an off-target response to the CRBN-binding module of QC-01-175 (pomalidomide).
source: Degradation of these C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors was expected as an off-target response to the CRBN-binding module of QC-01–175 (pomalidomide, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on known effects of pomalidomide and IMiDs on C2H2 zinc finger proteins.

claim: The negative control QC-03-075 (1 μM) revealed no effect on ZFP91, ZNF653 and ZNF827.
source: Conversely, the negative control QC-03–075 (1 μM) revealed no effect on these proteins, confirming the ablation of CRBN-binding activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Pre-treatment with MLN4924 and QC-01-175 showed a complete rescue of IMiD target degradation.
source: The degradation rescue experiment, consisting of pre-treatment with the neddylation inhibitor MLN4924 (inhibits activation of all NEDD8-dependent CRL) (Lan et al., 2016) and QC-01–175, showed a complete rescue of IMiD target degradation, confirming the neddylation and hence cullin-dependence for target degradation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: QC-01-175 has minimal off-target activity in the A152T neuronal proteome.
source: These results confirmed that QC-01–175 has minimal off-target activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Accumulation of tau and P-tau of reduced solubility in FTD patient-derived neuronal cell models is coupled to increased cellular vulnerability to specific forms of stress.
source: In FTD patient-derived neuronal cell models, accumulation of tau and P-tau of reduced solubility is coupled to increased cellular vulnerability to specific forms of stress (Silva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silva et al., 2016.

claim: The proteotoxicity caused by Aβ(1-42) promotes a concentration-dependent loss of viability in A152T and P301L neurons.
source: One of these stressors is the proteotoxicity caused by the highly aggregation-prone peptide Aβ(1-42), which promotes a concentration-dependent loss of viability in A152T and P301L neurons (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The effect of Aβ(1-42) on viability is not seen in WT control neurons.
source: This effect on viability is not seen in WT control neurons and can be rescued by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated MAPT knockout (KO) in A152T neurons (Figure 7A) (Silva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The effect of Aβ(1-42) on viability can be rescued by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated MAPT knockout in A152T neurons.
source: This effect on viability is not seen in WT control neurons and can be rescued by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated MAPT knockout (KO) in A152T neurons (Figure 7A) (Silva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Silva et al., 2016.

claim: Vehicle pre-treated A152T neurons followed by Aβ(1-42) treatment lost 50% viability at the 24 hr time-point.
source: Vehicle pre-treated neurons followed by Aβ(1-42) treatment loss 50% viability at the 24 hr time-point (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: QC-01-175 pre-treatment rescued viability to 90% of vehicle-alone control in A152T neurons treated with Aβ(1-42).
source: QC-01–175 pre-treatment rescued viability to 90% of vehicle-alone control, almost phenocopying the 100% viability rescue observed in MAPT KO neurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The negative control QC-03-075 had little effect on the toxicity of Aβ(1-42) in A152T neurons.
source: The negative control QC-03–075 had little effect on the toxicity of Aβ(1-42).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 24 hr treatment with either QC-01-175 or negative control alone caused no change in neuronal viability.
source: As expected, 24 hr treatment with either QC-01–175 or negative control alone caused no change in neuronal viability (Figure 7C, left blue bars).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The tau degrader QC-01-175 triggers proteasome-dependent tau and P-tau clearance in FTD patient-derived neurons.
source: In conclusion, the tau degrader QC-01–175 triggers proteasome-dependent tau and P-tau clearance in FTD patient-derived neurons, which is able to rescue tau-mediated toxicity in biologically relevant assays of stress vulnerability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: QC-01-175 is able to rescue tau-mediated toxicity in biologically relevant assays of stress vulnerability.
source: In conclusion, the tau degrader QC-01–175 triggers proteasome-dependent tau and P-tau clearance in FTD patient-derived neurons, which is able to rescue tau-mediated toxicity in biologically relevant assays of stress vulnerability.
evidence: This is supported by the viability assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Disease-relevant forms of tau and P-tau in FTD patient-derived neuronal cell models are amenable to targeted degradation.
source: In this study, we established that disease-relevant forms of tau and P-tau in FTD patient-derived neuronal cell models are amenable to targeted degradation and characterize the tool compound QC-01–175 as an effective tau degrader.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results showing tau degradation in FTD neurons.

claim: QC-01-175 is characterized as an effective tau degrader.
source: In this study, we established that disease-relevant forms of tau and P-tau in FTD patient-derived neuronal cell models are amenable to targeted degradation and characterize the tool compound QC-01–175 as an effective tau degrader.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results showing tau degradation by QC-01-175.

claim: E. coli-expressed and purified recombinant human tau has distinct properties that are not reflective of intracellular protein conformations.
source: E. coli-expressed and purified recombinant human tau has distinct properties that are not reflective of intracellular protein conformations, which may be key to the recognition, binding and degradation of tau by QC-01–175 in the neuronal context.
evidence: This is a known limitation of recombinant protein systems.

claim: Intracellular protein conformations may be key to the recognition, binding and degradation of tau by QC-01-175 in the neuronal context.
source: E. coli-expressed and purified recombinant human tau has distinct properties that are not reflective of intracellular protein conformations, which may be key to the recognition, binding and degradation of tau by QC-01–175 in the neuronal context.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in binding affinity observed in vitro versus cellular activity.

claim: Human stem cell-derived neurons allow access to physiologically relevant cell types and protein complexes.
source: Human stem cell-derived neurons allow access to physiologically relevant cell types and protein complexes, offering the advantage of modeling pathogenic tau species without the need for overexpression of heterologous genes, in the context of the patient genomic background (Dolmetsch and Geschwind, 2011; Silva et al., 2017; Wan et al., 2015; Chesselet and Carmichael, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on iPSC-derived neuronal models.

claim: The effect of QC-01-175 in A152T and P301L heterozygous neurons led on average to more than 70% and 60% clearance of tau, respectively, when only about 50% of tau expressed has the variant.
source: The effect of QC-01–175 in A152T and P301L heterozygous neurons led on average to more than 70% and 60% clearance of tau, respectively, when only about 50% of tau expressed has the variant.
evidence: This is supported by the degradation data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Some forms of non-mutant tau in FTD neurons are also misfolded and targeted for degradation by QC-01-175.
source: This is informative regarding the species of tau targeted by the degrader, raising the hypothesis that some forms of non-mutant tau in FTD neurons are also misfolded and targeted for degradation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that degradation exceeds 50% in heterozygous neurons.

claim: It may be possible to develop tau-degrader therapies that selectively act in FTD-affected neurons, and on disease-associated forms of tau, independent of genotype, and spare normal tau protein.
source: Remarkably, the degrader preferentially targeted tau species from FTD neurons, with minimal effect on tau from unaffected WT control neurons. This indicates that it may be possible to develop tau-degrader therapies that selectively act in FTD-affected neurons, and on disease-associated forms of tau, independent of genotype, and spare normal tau protein within the affected regions of the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the therapeutic potential based on the observed selectivity.

claim: Variation in QC-01-175-mediated tau degradation dose profiles between A152T and P301L neurons points to differences in tau species originated by the two tau variants.
source: Variation in QC-01–175-mediated tau degradation dose profiles between A152T and P301L neurons (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) points to differences in tau species originated by the two tau variants, and possibly also differences in proteostasis for the two patient-derived cell models, which affects UPS function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in degradation profiles shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Differences in proteostasis for the two patient-derived cell models may affect UPS function.
source: Variation in QC-01–175-mediated tau degradation dose profiles between A152T and P301L neurons (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) points to differences in tau species originated by the two tau variants, and possibly also differences in proteostasis for the two patient-derived cell models, which affects UPS function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential differences in cellular proteostasis.

claim: The proteasome has been demonstrated to be affected by neurodegeneration and aging.
source: This aspect will impact the clinical translational potential of any degrader targeting tau to the proteasome, which has been demonstrated to be affected by neurodegeneration and aging itself (Deger et al., 2015; Keck et al., 2003; Saez and Vilchez, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on proteasome function in aging and neurodegeneration.

claim: Targeted degraders may be developed as therapeutic strategies for early stage disease, or as a co-therapeutic with proteasome activity chemical enhancers.
source: This, however, does not preclude the development of targeted degraders as therapeutic strategies for early stage disease, or as a co-therapeutic with proteasome activity chemical enhancers (Myeku and Duff, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic strategies.

claim: There may be a basal level of interaction between tau and the CRL4CRBN E3 ligase in A152T neurons.
source: Notably, co-IP results (Figure 4) suggest that there is a basal level of interaction between tau and the CRL4CRBN E3 ligase in A152T neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In FTD there may be some basal tau:CRBN association.
source: Interestingly, Del Prete et al. reported that tau could be a natural substrate of CRBN through a complex involving the amyloid precursor protein (APP), mutations in which are known to cause AD (Del Prete et al., 2016). The co-IP experiment data we present here indicates that in FTD there may also be some basal tau:CRBN association, and thus, rather than targeting a 'neo-substrate', QC-01–175 may be promoting efficacy of a physiological process, increasing the probability of successful tau degradation in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data and supported by citation to Del Prete et al., 2016.

claim: QC-01-175 may be promoting efficacy of a physiological process rather than targeting a 'neo-substrate'.
source: Interestingly, Del Prete et al. reported that tau could be a natural substrate of CRBN through a complex involving the amyloid precursor protein (APP), mutations in which are known to cause AD (Del Prete et al., 2016). The co-IP experiment data we present here indicates that in FTD there may also be some basal tau:CRBN association, and thus, rather than targeting a 'neo-substrate', QC-01–175 may be promoting efficacy of a physiological process, increasing the probability of successful tau degradation in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed basal interaction.

claim: QC-01-175 is a relatively large and flexible molecule compared to most brain-active drugs and may suffer from fast metabolism and poor brain penetration.
source: From a pharmacology standpoint, QC-01–175 is a relatively large and flexible molecule compared to most brain-active drugs and may suffer from fast metabolism and poor brain penetration.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential pharmacological challenges based on the structure of QC-01-175.

claim: Tuning pharmacology for in vivo applications is an ongoing challenge in the targeted protein degradation field, but progress is being made.
source: Tuning pharmacology for in vivo applications is an ongoing challenge in the targeted protein degradation field, but progress is being made (Gu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gu et al., 2018.

claim: If pharmacology tuning proves intractable, intrathecal administration could be considered for QC-01-175.
source: If this tuning proves intractable, intrathecal administration could be considered.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative administration routes.

claim: It might be possible to use PET to measure target engagement of QC-01-175 in vivo.
source: Since QC-01–175 occupies the binding site of a PET ligand, it might be possible to use PET to measure target engagement in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential biomarker strategies.

claim: Degraders can act catalytically, and their pharmacodynamics may influence and complicate PET readings.
source: However, because degraders can act catalytically, their pharmacodynamics may influence and complicate PET readings.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential complications with PET imaging of degraders.

claim: Three C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors were downregulated by a 4 hr treatment with QC-01-175 in A152T neurons.
source: The degrader can recognize and downregulate other proteins as shown here by mass spectrometry global proteome analysis (Figure 6A), where three C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors were downregulated by a 4 hr treatment with QC-01–175.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: This off-target activity likely arises from the CRBN-binding module of QC-01-175 (pomalidomide).
source: This off-target activity likely arises from the CRBN-binding module of QC-01–175 (pomalidomide, Figure 1C), which has been reported to induce degradation of multiple members of the C2H2 zinc finger protein family through a 'molecular glue' type mechanism (Sievers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sievers et al., 2018.

claim: Efforts to design next generation tau degraders will involve tuning the attachment chemistry to replace the aniline nitrogen, and altering the degrader linker composition to remove IMiD off-target effects.
source: Using what is known about IMiD-based degrader design, efforts to design next generation tau degraders will involve tuning the attachment chemistry to replace the aniline nitrogen, and altering the degrader linker composition to remove these IMiD off-target effects (Nowak et al., 2018; Dobrovolsky et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2019), thus creating a tau-selective degrader.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on IMiD-based degrader design.

claim: QC-01-175 may have modulatory effect on function/activity of other proteins without leading to degradation.
source: However, QC-01–175 may also have modulatory effect on function/activity of other proteins without leading to degradation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential off-target effects.

claim: A detailed profiling of off-target binding interactions is a necessary future investigative effort for QC-01-175.
source: Therefore, a detailed profiling of off-target binding interactions is a necessary future investigative effort.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: An interesting strategy for clinical trial success might be to screen individual patients for responsiveness using cellular models.
source: Finally, since it is now possible to routinely establish patient specific iPSC-derived neuronal cultures, an interesting strategy for clinical trial success might be to screen individual patients for responsiveness using cellular models.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical trial strategies.

claim: A neurodegeneration-specific workflow for development of targeted degraders for aggregation-prone proteins has been established.
source: In conclusion, here we have established a neurodegeneration-specific workflow for development of targeted degraders for aggregation-prone proteins.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the overall approach described in the manuscript.

claim: The workflow leveraged existing PET probe binders in degrader design, and well-characterized patient-derived neuronal models to assay against clinically relevant protein species and phenotypes.
source: Our workflow leveraged existing PET probe binders in degrader design, and well-characterized patient-derived neuronal models to assay against clinically relevant protein species and phenotypes.
evidence: This describes the approach used in the study.

claim: QC-01-175 is a valuable new research tool for the study of tau-mediated events in human tauopathies.
source: These efforts yielded QC-01–175, a valuable new research tool for the study of tau-mediated events in human tauopathies.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of QC-01-175 as a research tool.

claim: PET-tracer-based hetero-bifunctional degrader design and patient-derived cellular models offer an unprecedented advantage for the targeting of pathologically relevant tau species.
source: PET-tracer-based hetero-bifunctional degrader design and patient-derived cellular models offer an unprecedented advantage for the targeting of pathologically relevant tau species, relative to in vitro and heterologous expression systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the advantages of the approach used in this study.

claim: Future advances in understanding the relationship between tau post-translational modifications and adopted conformations in disease will aid in the knowledge-based design of next generation targeted degraders.
source: Additionally, we anticipate that future advances in understanding the relationship between tau post-translational modifications and adopted conformations in disease, as well as visualizing and modeling interactions between tau and various PET tracers, will aid in the knowledge-based design of next generation targeted degraders.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: The approach may be generalizable to other proteinopathies where high-quality PET tracers and cellular models are available.
source: Importantly, our approach may be generalizable to other proteinopathies where high-quality PET tracers and cellular models are available.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader applicability of the approach.

claim: Small-molecule-mediated protein degradation represents a promising strategy to advance our understanding of human neurodegenerative disease and translate those insights into targeted therapies.
source: In this context, our study suggests that small-molecule-mediated protein degradation represents a promising strategy to advance our understanding of human neurodegenerative disease and translate those insights into targeted therapies.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the potential of the degrader approach.
